front: State Cummings' definitions of even and odd integers (Definition 2.2).
back: An integer n is even if n = 2k for some integer k; n is odd if n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. — Cummings §2.1, Definition 2.2, p. 37

front: What is a direct proof, in Cummings' own words?
back: "A direct proof is a way to prove a 'P ⇒ Q' proposition by starting with P and working your way to Q." — Cummings §2 ("The Structure of Direct Proofs"), p. 41

front: State Theorem 5.14 (the contrapositive equivalence) precisely.
back: An implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive: (P ⇒ Q) ⇔ (¬Q ⇒ ¬P). — Cummings §5, Theorem 5.14, p. 198

front: Which proof technique cracks "n² even ⇒ n even" cleanly, and why does direct proof struggle with it?
back: Contrapositive. Direct proof stalls because the hypothesis talks about n² and the conclusion wants n — there's no clean algebraic way to "un-square" 2k into 2j. The contrapositive (n odd ⇒ n² odd) matches algebra's natural direction instead. — Cummings §2.1 p. 37 (the snag); §6.2 pp. 201–203 (the fix)

front: What must a contrapositive proof do at its close that a direct proof does not need to, and why?
back: It must explicitly invoke the contrapositive equivalence (Theorem 5.14) in the closing sentence — because, taken at face value, a contrapositive argument proves ¬Q ⇒ ¬P, a *different* statement from P ⇒ Q; only that closing invocation licenses the connection. — Cummings §6.2, footnote 6, p. 203

front: What is the logical shape of a proof by contradiction, and which classic theorem is its show-piece example?
back: Assume P true and Q false simultaneously, then derive an unconditionally false statement (an absurdity); since true assumptions can't yield falsity via valid logic, the assumption must be rotten. Show-piece: Hippasus' proof that √2 is irrational (Theorem 7.6). — Cummings §7, p. 215; §7.3, Theorem 7.6, pp. 225–226

front: Outline the proof strategy for "√2 is irrational" by contradiction.
back:
- Assume for contradiction √2 = p/q in lowest terms (p, q nonzero integers, no common divisor)
- Square both sides: 2q² = p², so 2 | p², hence 2 | p (p = 2k)
- Substitute and simplify: q² = 2k², so 2 | q² and hence 2 | q
- Contradiction: p and q are both even, violating "lowest terms"
- Conclude √2 cannot be rational — Cummings §7.3, Theorem 7.6, pp. 225–226

front: Outline the proof strategy for "the sum of two even integers is even" (Proposition 2.4).
back:
- Assume n, m even; write n = 2a, m = 2b by Definition 2.2
- Add: n + m = 2a + 2b = 2(a+b)
- Note a+b is an integer, so n+m matches the form 2k
- Conclude n+m is even by Definition 2.2 — Cummings §2.1, Proposition 2.4, p. 38

front: Outline the proof strategy for "there is no largest even integer", and say which technique it uses.
back:
Contradiction (triggered by the non-existence claim "there is no..."):
- Assume for contradiction a largest even integer N exists
- Construct N + 2, also even
- Show N + 2 > N, contradicting N's maximality
- Conclude no largest even integer exists — Cummings §7, Proposition 7.1 (cf. heuristic synthesis, §6.2 p. 202–203 and §7 pp. 213–215)

front: State Cummings' Principle 4.1 (ordinary Induction).
back: Consider statements S₁, S₂, S₃, … Suppose S₁ is true, and suppose for each k ∈ ℕ, if S_k is true then S_{k+1} is true. Then S_n is true for every n ∈ ℕ. — Cummings §4.1, Principle 4.1, p. 108

front: State Cummings' Principle 4.7 (Strong Induction).
back: Suppose S₁ is true, and suppose for any k ∈ ℕ, if S₁, S₂, …, S_k are all true, then S_{k+1} is true. Then S_n is true for every n ∈ ℕ. — Cummings §4.3, Principle 4.7, p. 125

front: State the well-ordering principle for ℕ, and why it fails for the positive rationals.
back: Every non-empty set of natural numbers contains a smallest element. It fails for the positive rationals because halving any candidate "smallest" positive rational produces a strictly smaller one — there's no floor, unlike ℕ where 1 genuinely is one. — Cummings §7, p. 233 (footnote on minimal-counterexample technique); pw-02 §2, contrast with ℚ

front: What are the four required labelled parts of any induction proof, per Cummings, and which closing phrase is non-negotiable?
back: Base Case (show S₁ directly); Inductive Hypothesis (assume S_k for fixed but arbitrary k); Induction Step (prove S_k ⟹ S_{k+1}); Conclusion — the phrase "therefore, by induction, S_n holds for all n ∈ ℕ" is required, not decoration: without it you've shown two separate finite facts, not the infinite chain. — Cummings §4.1, p. 108; §4.2, p. 115

front: Why did the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic proof need strong induction rather than ordinary induction?
back: Knowing k is prime or a product of primes says almost nothing directly about k+1. But if k+1 is composite, k+1 = st with s, t both smaller than k+1 (not necessarily equal to k) — so the proof needs access to whichever earlier case s and t happen to land on, which is strong induction's signature move. — Cummings §4.3, Theorem 4.8 and discussion, pp. 126–127

front: How are induction, strong induction, and well-ordering related as logical statements about ℕ?
back: They are logically equivalent — each can be shown to imply the next in a cycle (well-ordering ⟹ induction ⟹ strong induction ⟹ well-ordering), so all three certify exactly the same underlying structural fact about how ℕ is built. — pw-02 heuristic sketch, synthesising Cummings Ch. 4 and §7, p. 233

front: Outline the induction proof strategy for 1 + 2 + ⋯ + n = n(n+1)/2 (Proposition 4.2).
back:
- Base case n=1: LHS=1, RHS=1(2)/2=1, equal
- Inductive hypothesis: assume 1+⋯+k = k(k+1)/2 for fixed but arbitrary k
- Induction step: split off the last term, 1+⋯+k+(k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1), then do the algebra to reach (k+1)(k+2)/2
- Conclude "therefore, by induction..." for all n ∈ ℕ — Cummings §4.2, Proposition 4.2, pp. 110–112

front: Outline the strong-induction proof strategy for the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (every n ≥ 2 is prime or a product of primes).
back:
- Base case n=2: prime, done immediately
- Inductive hypothesis: assume every integer 2,…,k is prime or a product of primes
- Induction step on k+1: if prime, done; if composite, write k+1 = st with 1<s,t<k+1, both covered by the hypothesis, so each factors into primes
- Concatenate s's and t's factorisations to get k+1's factorisation
- Conclude by strong induction — Cummings §4.3, Theorem 4.8, pp. 126–127

front: Outline how well-ordering is used to prove ordinary induction holds (the "well-ordering ⟹ induction" direction).
back:
- Suppose S₁ true and S_k ⟹ S_{k+1} for every k, but some S_n false
- Let F = {n : S_n false}, assumed non-empty
- By well-ordering, F has a smallest element m; since S₁ true, m ≠ 1
- Minimality of m forces S_{m-1} true, so the inductive step forces S_m true — contradicting m ∈ F
- Conclude F is empty, so induction holds — pw-02 heuristic sketch (standard textbook argument), Cummings Ch. 4 context

front: State Axler's definition of a vector space (Definition 1.19).
back: A set V with an addition and scalar multiplication satisfying: commutativity (u+v=v+u); associativity ((u+v)+w=u+(v+w), (ab)v=a(bv)); additive identity (∃0∈V, v+0=v); additive inverse (∀v∃w, v+w=0); multiplicative identity (1v=v); distributive properties (a(u+v)=au+av, (a+b)v=av+bv). — Axler §1.B, Definition 1.19, pp. 12–13

front: What does Axler's Notation 1.6 mean by the symbol F, and why is it useful?
back: F stands for either R or C throughout the book. A theorem proved "for F" is automatically proved twice — once for the reals, once for the complex numbers — for free. — Axler §1.A, Notation 1.6, p. 4

front: Define Fᴧ S (Axler's function-space notation) and state which two earlier examples are special cases of it.
back: F^S is the set of all functions from a set S to F, with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. Fⁿ = F^{1,…,n} and F^∞ = F^{1,2,…} are both special cases of F^S — lists and sequences are secretly just functions from an index set to F. — Axler §1.B, Notation 1.23 and Example 1.24, pp. 13–14

front: What must you check to show 0v = 0 for every vector v (Theorem 1.29), and what is notable about this fact given the definition of vector space?
back: 0v = (0+0)v = 0v + 0v by distributivity; adding −(0v) to both sides gives 0 = 0v. It's notable because nothing about "what the elements of V are" is used — the fact follows purely from the axioms, for any vector space whatsoever. — Axler §1.B, Theorem 1.29, p. 16

front: Does Definition 1.19 require the elements of a vector space to be lists, arrows, or tuples of numbers?
back: No — the definition says nothing about what the elements "are", only how addition and scalar multiplication must behave. This is exactly why function spaces, sequence spaces, and even the one-point set {0} all qualify as vector spaces. — Axler §1.B, Definition 1.20 and discussion, p. 13

front: State Theorem 1.25 and give the one-line proof idea.
back: A vector space has a unique additive identity. Proof idea: if 0 and 0′ are both additive identities, then 0′ = 0′+0 = 0+0′ = 0, using each one's identity property plus commutativity, so 0′ = 0. — Axler §1.B, Theorem 1.25, p. 15

front: Outline the proof strategy for commutativity of addition in Fⁿ (Theorem 1.13).
back:
- Write x, y as coordinate lists (x₁,…,xₙ), (y₁,…,yₙ)
- Apply the definition of addition in Fⁿ to get (x₁+y₁,…,xₙ+yₙ)
- Use commutativity of addition already known in F, coordinate by coordinate
- Rewrite as (y₁+x₁,…,yₙ+xₙ) = y+x — Axler §1.A, Theorem 1.13, p. 6

front: Outline the proof strategy for uniqueness of the additive identity (Theorem 1.25).
back:
- Suppose 0 and 0′ are both additive identities for the same V
- Compute 0′ + 0 two ways: using 0 as identity gives 0′+0 = 0′; using commutativity and 0′ as identity gives 0+0′ = 0
- Chain the equalities: 0′ = 0′+0 = 0+0′ = 0
- Conclude 0′ = 0, so the identity is unique — Axler §1.B, Theorem 1.25, p. 15

front: State Axler's definition of a subspace (Definition 1.32).
back: A subset U of V is called a subspace of V if U is also a vector space, using the same addition and scalar multiplication as on V. — Axler §1.C, Definition 1.32, p. 18

front: State Axler's definition of a direct sum (Definition 1.40).
back: The sum U₁ + ⋯ + Uₘ (of subspaces) is called a direct sum if each element of the sum can be written in only one way as u₁+⋯+uₘ with each uⱼ ∈ Uⱼ. Written U₁ ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ Uₘ. — Axler §1.C, Definition 1.40, p. 21

front: State the sum of subspaces (Definition 1.36), and how it differs from a plain union.
back: U₁+⋯+Uₘ = {u₁+⋯+uₘ : uⱼ ∈ Uⱼ}. Unlike a union, the sum stays closed under addition and hence is itself a subspace — in fact the smallest subspace containing all the Uⱼ; "the union of subspaces is rarely a subspace" itself. — Axler §1.C, Definition 1.36, p. 20; Theorem 1.39, pp. 20–21

front: State Theorem 1.34 (the subspace test) — the three conditions to check.
back: U ⊆ V is a subspace iff: (1) 0 ∈ U (additive identity); (2) u,w ∈ U ⟹ u+w ∈ U (closed under addition); (3) a ∈ F, u ∈ U ⟹ au ∈ U (closed under scalar multiplication). — Axler §1.C, Theorem 1.34, pp. 18–19

front: State Theorem 1.45 (the two-subspace direct-sum test), and note its key limitation.
back: For two subspaces U, W of V: U+W is a direct sum iff U ∩ W = {0}. Key limitation: this clean intersection test is a genuine special privilege of exactly two subspaces — for three or more, pairwise {0}-intersections are not sufficient (Example 1.43). — Axler §1.C, Theorem 1.45, p. 23; discussion p. 24

front: Which linear equation form is the classic "offset trap" that usually breaks a subspace attempt, and why?
back: A linear but inhomogeneous defining equation with a leftover constant (e.g. x₃ = 5x₄ + b with b ≠ 0). It almost never contains the zero vector unless b = 0, since 0 must satisfy 0 = 5·0 + b, forcing b = 0 — so the additive-identity condition of Theorem 1.34 fails instantly whenever b ≠ 0. — Axler §1.C, Example 1.35(a), p. 19

front: Outline the proof strategy showing F³ = U ⊕ W for U = {(x,y,0)}, W = {(0,0,z)} (Example 1.41).
back:
- Show the sum equals F³: any (x,y,z) = (x,y,0)+(0,0,z), one summand from each
- Invoke Theorem 1.44: directness reduces to checking 0 decomposes uniquely
- Suppose 0 = u+w with u=(a,b,0)∈U, w=(0,0,c)∈W; then (a,b,c)=(0,0,0) forces a=b=c=0
- Conclude the only decomposition of 0 is trivial, so F³ = U⊕W — Axler §1.C, Example 1.41, p. 21

front: Outline why U₁+U₂+U₃ = F³ but the sum is not direct in Axler's Example 1.43.
back:
- Show the sum fills F³: any (x,y,z) = (x,y,0)+(0,0,z)+(0,0,0)
- Invoke Theorem 1.44: exhibit a second, non-trivial way to write 0 as u₁+u₂+u₃
- Pick u₃=(0,1,1)∈U₃, then find u₁∈U₁ and u₂∈U₂ that cancel it, giving a second decomposition of 0
- Conclude 0 has two distinct decompositions, so the sum is not direct despite filling the whole space — Axler §1.C, Example 1.43, pp. 21–22

front: State the Axiom of Completeness (Abbott).
back: Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound. — Abbott §1.3, p. 14

front: State Abbott's definition of supremum (Definition 1.3.2).
back: A real number s is the least upper bound (supremum, sup A) for A ⊆ ℝ if: (i) s is an upper bound for A, and (ii) if b is any upper bound for A, then s ≤ b. Infimum is defined the same way for lower bounds. — Abbott §1.3, Definition 1.3.2, p. 14

front: State Theorem 1.1.1 and note what makes it historically significant.
back: There is no rational number whose square is 2. Significant because it broke the Pythagorean assumption that any two lengths share a common rational sub-unit — showing "number" (as rational) is strictly weaker than geometric length. — Abbott §1.1, Theorem 1.1.1, p. 2; discussion p. 3

front: True or false, with reasoning: sup A must always be an element of A.
back: False. E.g. sup(0,2) = 2, but 2 ∉ (0,2) — supremum is a bound, not necessarily a member. When the supremum does belong to A, it's also the maximum, but that's a bonus, not a requirement. — Abbott §1.3, Example 1.3.5, p. 15

front: Why doesn't the Axiom of Completeness need to separately assert existence of greatest lower bounds?
back: Because inf A can be recovered as −sup(−A): given A bounded below, the set of its lower bounds is bounded above, and its supremum equals inf A. One axiom secures both directions for free. — Abbott §1.3, p. 16, and Exercise 1.3.3

front: Why is ℚ densely packed yet still not complete? What crucial distinction does this reveal?
back: Density (between any two rationals sits another) only guarantees arbitrarily close approximation — not that the limit itself is rational. √2 can be approximated to any precision within ℚ, yet no rational number equals it: there's a "hole" in the rational line. Dense ≠ complete. — Abbott §1.1, p. 4

front: Outline the proof strategy for "there is no rational number whose square is 2" (Theorem 1.1.1).
back:
- Assume for contradiction p/q in lowest terms with (p/q)²=2
- Derive p²=2q², so p² even, hence p even; write p=2r
- Substitute: 2r²=q², so q² even, hence q even
- Contradiction: p and q both even, violating lowest terms — Abbott §1.1, Theorem 1.1.1, pp. 1–2

front: Outline the proof strategy for showing sup A = 1 where A = {1/n : n ∈ ℕ} (Example 1.3.3).
back:
- Check part (i): 1 is an upper bound, since 1/n ≤ 1 for every n ≥ 1
- Check part (ii): let b be any upper bound; since 1 ∈ A (take n=1), b being an upper bound forces 1 ≤ b
- Both conditions of Definition 1.3.2 hold
- Conclude sup A = 1 — Abbott §1.3, Example 1.3.3, p. 15

front: Outline how the Axiom of Completeness is used to prove a real number α with α² = 2 exists (Theorem 1.4.5).
back:
- Define T = {t ∈ ℝ : t² < 2}, nonempty and bounded above
- By Completeness, α = sup T exists
- Rule out α² < 2 (would let you nudge α slightly larger, still in T — contradicting sup)
- Rule out α² > 2 (would let you find a smaller upper bound — contradicting least upper bound)
- Conclude α² = 2 exactly — Abbott §1.4, Theorem 1.4.5, pp. 21–22

front: State Abbott's definition of cardinality equivalence (Definition 1.4.7) and of countable (Definition 1.4.10).
back: A ∼ B if there exists f: A→B that is 1–1 and onto (a bijection). A set A is countable if ℕ ∼ A; an infinite set that is not countable is uncountable. — Abbott §1.4, Definitions 1.4.7 and 1.4.10, pp. 23–24

front: State Abbott's definitions of one-to-one and onto (Definition 1.4.6).
back: f: A→B is one-to-one (1–1) if a₁≠a₂ in A implies f(a₁)≠f(a₂) in B. It is onto if for every b∈B there exists a∈A with f(a)=b. — Abbott §1.4, Definition 1.4.6, p. 23

front: State Cantor's Theorem (Theorem 1.5.2) about power sets.
back: Given any set A, there does not exist a function f: A → P(A) that is onto. — Abbott §1.5, Theorem 1.5.2, p. 32

front: ℕ ∼ E, the even naturals, even though E is a proper subset of ℕ. What does this reveal about infinite sets?
back: Being a proper subset says nothing about relative cardinality once sets are infinite — a set can have the same cardinality as one of its own proper subsets (f(n)=2n is a bijection ℕ→E). Finite-set intuition ("proper subset must be strictly smaller") fails here. — Abbott §1.4, Example 1.4.8, p. 23

front: In the shell-listing proof that ℚ is countable, why does each shell Aₙ need to be finite?
back: You can only concatenate the shells into one well-defined ℕ-indexed list if each shell finishes before the next starts. If some shell were infinite, you'd never finish listing it and so never reach the next one. — Abbott §1.4, Theorem 1.4.11(i), pp. 24–26

front: Why must the diagonal argument compare bₙ against the diagonal entry aₙₙ specifically, rather than a fixed column like aₙ₁?
back: Only the diagonal supplies a distinct, dedicated disagreement slot for every single row. A fixed column would only defeat rows whose digit happens to match that column — it wouldn't guarantee disagreement with every f(n) individually. — Abbott §1.5, Theorem 1.5.1, pp. 29–31

front: Outline the proof strategy for Theorem 1.5.1: (0,1) is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument).
back:
- Assume for contradiction f: ℕ→(0,1) is onto, listing every real in (0,1) as decimal expansions
- Build adversary x = .b₁b₂b₃… using rule bₙ = 2 if aₙₙ≠2, else 3 (diagonal digits, deliberately disagreeing)
- Note x ∈ (0,1) but x differs from f(n) at digit n, for every n
- So x is missing from a list assumed exhaustive — contradiction
- Conclude no such onto f exists; (0,1) is uncountable — Abbott §1.5, Theorem 1.5.1, pp. 29–31

front: Outline the proof strategy that ℚ is countable via the shell-listing method (Theorem 1.4.11(i)).
back:
- Group rationals into finite shells Aₙ by |p|+|q| in lowest terms (n∈ℕ)
- Note each Aₙ is finite, and every rational lands in exactly one shell
- List shells one after another: all of A₁, then A₂, then A₃, …
- This concatenated list contains every rational exactly once
- The list itself is the required bijection with ℕ — Abbott §1.4, Theorem 1.4.11(i), pp. 24–26

front: State Carter's four informal Rules (1.5–1.8) that define "a system of actions" before the formal group axioms appear.
back: Rule 1.5: a fixed list of moves that never changes. Rule 1.6: every action is reversible. Rule 1.7: every action is deterministic (no randomness). Rule 1.8: any sequence of consecutive actions is also an action. — Carter §1.4, pp. 6–7

front: What is the Klein 4-group, and which two physically different puzzles does Carter show share it?
back: The abstract structure shared by the rectangle's four flip-configurations and two independent light switches' four on/off configurations — same map of configurations and moves, just relabelled. Named the Klein 4-group. — Carter §2.5, pp. 19–20

front: How many distinct configurations does the rectangle puzzle (two flips: horizontal, vertical) have in total, and why exactly that many?
back: Four: solved, horizontal-flipped, vertical-flipped, and both together (the half-turn). Flipping twice in either direction returns to an already-visited state; combining both flips gives one genuinely new fourth state, and nothing beyond that appears. — Carter §2.3, pp. 15–18

front: Why do the rectangle puzzle and the two-light-switch puzzle count as "the same group" despite being physically different?
back: Group theory studies the pattern of how actions combine, not the physical material carrying them out. Their maps of configurations-and-moves (Cayley diagrams) have identical structure, just different labels — strip away the rectangle-ness or switch-ness and the same abstract skeleton (Klein 4-group) remains. — Carter §2.5, pp. 19–20

front: Which of Carter's rules guarantees that a combination not on the original generator list (e.g. flip-horizontal-then-flip-vertical) still counts as a legitimate group move?
back: Rule 1.8 — any sequence of consecutive actions is also an action. The generators are a starting point for building the whole group, not a ceiling on what counts as a move. — Carter §1.4, Rule 1.8, p. 6

front: Outline how Carter informally establishes that the rectangle puzzle's "do-nothing" move is a legitimate action on par with the two flips.
back:
- Note every rectangle configuration count must include the case where corners haven't moved ("reset")
- Observe Rule 1.8 lets "flip horizontal, then flip horizontal again" be treated as one combined action
- That combined action changes nothing, so it counts as a valid action by the rules already stated
- This "changes-nothing" action is later formalised as the identity — Carter §2.3, discovered fact 1, p. 15 (formalised aa-23, Aluffi Definition 11.1)

front: Outline the reasoning that establishes every rectangle-puzzle move has an "undo" (inverse), informally, before any axioms are stated.
back:
- For each of the four configurations, exhibit another move (possibly the same one) that returns to solved
- Horizontal flip undoes itself (flip again); vertical flip undoes itself likewise
- The 180° rotation (horizontal-then-vertical) is undone by repeating the same combination
- Note that in this particular group, every move happens to be its own undo — not true of every group — Carter §2.3, discovered fact 2, p. 15 (formalised aa-23 as inverses)

front: State Aluffi's formal group definition (Definition 11.1).
back: A group (G,·) is a set G with a binary operation · such that: (i) associativity (g·h)·k = g·(h·k); (ii) identity ∃eG ∈G ∀g: g·eG=eG·g=g; (iii) inverse ∀g ∃h: g·h=h·g=eG. Closure is built into "a binary operation on G". — Aluffi, Definition 11.1, pp. 229–230

front: State Aluffi's definition of the order of an element (Definition 10.12).
back: The order of g ∈ G, written |g|, is the cardinality of the cyclic group ⟨g⟩ = {gⁱ : i ∈ ℤ} generated by g. — Aluffi, Definition 10.12, p. 261

front: What does it mean to say a group is abelian, and give an example from aa-23.
back: A group is abelian if its operation is commutative: a·b = b·a for all a, b. Example: (ℤ, +) is abelian, since ordinary addition of integers commutes. — Aluffi §11.1, p. 231

front: Which single phrase in Definition 11.1 does the job that Carter's Rule 1.8 (combinations are also actions) did informally in aa-00?
back: The phrase "a binary operation on G" — this is closure: g·h always lands back inside G, symbolically encoding what Rule 1.8 stated informally. — Aluffi, Definition 11.1, p. 229

front: Which axiom of Definition 11.1 forces every row and column of a Cayley table to contain each group element exactly once, and why?
back: Axiom (iii), existence of inverses. If element x appeared twice in row g (g·h₁=g·h₂=x, h₁≠h₂), multiplying both sides on the left by g⁻¹ forces h₁=h₂ — a contradiction. So no repeats occur (the Latin square property). — Aluffi §11.1, discussion following Definition 11.1, p. 230

front: What structural fact distinguishes ℤ/4ℤ from the Klein four-group V₄, even though both have four elements?
back: ℤ/4ℤ has an element of order 4 (e.g. [1]), while every non-identity element of V₄ has order 2 (each is its own inverse). Same size, different internal clockwork — the groups are not relabellings of each other. — Aluffi §11.1, Definition 10.12 and Cayley table comparison, pp. 230, 261

front: Outline the proof strategy for uniqueness of the identity element in a group.
back:
- Suppose e₁ and e₂ both satisfy axiom (ii) for the same G
- Combine e₁ with e₂ using e₁'s identity property: e₁·e₂ = e₂
- Combine e₁ with e₂ using e₂'s identity property: e₁·e₂ = e₁
- Both compute the same expression e₁·e₂, so e₁ = e₂ — Aluffi §11.1, p. 230 (proof expanded from bullet observation)

front: Outline the proof strategy for uniqueness of inverses in a group (the "sandwich" strategy).
back:
- Suppose h₁ and h₂ both satisfy axiom (iii) as inverses of the same g
- Bracket h₁·g·h₂ on the left: (h₁·g)·h₂ = eG·h₂ = h₂
- Bracket the same expression on the right: h₁·(g·h₂) = h₁·eG = h₁
- By associativity these two bracketings compute the same element, so h₁ = h₂ — Aluffi §11.1, p. 230 (faded proof, standard sandwich strategy)
